content: Bacterial vaginosis is a condition characterized by an imbalance in the normal vaginal flora, with an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria and a reduction in the normal lactobacillary flora. While some women may experience symptoms such as a distinct vaginal discharge, many remain asymptomatic. During pregnancy, bacterial vaginosis has been linked to adverse perinatal outcomes, particularly preterm birth (PTB). Identifying and treating bacterial vaginosis during pregnancy may help mitigate the risk of PTB and its associated complications. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of antibiotic treatment for bacterial vaginosis in pregnant women. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, reviewed references from relevant articles, and examined abstracts, letters, and editorials. They included randomized controlled trials that compared antibiotic treatment with either placebo or no treatment, as well as trials comparing different antibiotic regimens in pregnant women with bacterial vaginosis or intermediate vaginal flora, regardless of whether they were symptomatic or asymptomatic. A total of 21 high-quality trials involving 7,847 pregnant women diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis or intermediate vaginal flora were included in the analysis. Antibiotic therapy was found to be effective in eradicating bacterial vaginosis during pregnancy, with a significant reduction in the risk of bacterial vaginosis recurrence (average risk ratio [RR] 0.42; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31 to 0.56). Additionally, antibiotic treatment was associated with a reduced risk of late miscarriage (RR 0.20; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.76). However, treatment did not significantly reduce the risk of PTB before 37 weeks of gestation (average RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.71 to 1.09) or the risk of preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.30 to 1.84). Antibiotic treatment was associated with an increased risk of side effects severe enough to necessitate discontinuation or modification of the treatment regimen (RR 1.66; 95% CI 1.02 to 2.68). When treatment was initiated before 20 weeks of gestation, it did not significantly reduce the risk of PTB before 37 weeks (average RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.17). In women with a history of PTB, antibiotic treatment did not significantly alter the risk of subsequent PTB (average RR 0.78; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.48). However, in women with abnormal vaginal flora (including intermediate flora or bacterial vaginosis), treatment was associated with a reduced risk of PTB before 37 weeks (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.34 to 0.84). One small trial involving 156 women compared oral and vaginal formulations of metronidazole and clindamycin. No significant differences were observed in the primary outcomes, but small differences were noted in gestational age prolongation (mean difference [MD] 1.00 days; 95% CI 0.26 to 1.74) and birthweight (MD 75.18 grams; 95% CI 25.37 to 124.99 grams), which were not clinically significant. Oral antibiotics did not reduce the risk of PTB compared to vaginal antibiotics (RR 1.09; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.52). However, oral antibiotics showed some advantages over vaginal antibiotics in terms of neonatal unit admission (RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.42 to 0.92), gestational age prolongation (MD 9.00 days; 95% CI 8.20 to 9.80), and birthweight (MD 342.13 grams; 95% CI 293.04 to 391.22). A single small trial assessed different dosing frequencies of antibiotics and found no significant differences in outcomes. In conclusion, antibiotic treatment is effective in eradicating bacterial vaginosis during pregnancy. However, it does not significantly reduce the overall risk of PTB. The evidence does not support routine screening and treatment of all pregnant women with bacterial vaginosis to prevent PTB and its associated complications. When the screening criteria were expanded to include women with abnormal vaginal flora, a 47% reduction in PTB was observed, but this finding was based on only two studies.
